source.title: Implicit Regularization of Stochastic Gradient Descent in Natural Language Processing: Observations and Implications
source.authors: Deren Lei; Zi-Chen Sun; Yijun Xiao; William Yang Wang

record.file_problem: not stated; the supplied text appears to contain the full paper, including references.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how partial label corruption affects generalization in NLP models, a related question to the claim, but does not reproduce the original random-label fitting experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Zhang et al. (2016) for fitting random labels; that cited result is not this study's result. Its own corrupted-label experiment reports generalization behavior, but not whether the models fit each corrupted training set perfectly. The batch-size and dropout results on true labels do not establish whether those methods prevent fitting random labels.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own NLP results on test performance under increasing label corruption (V4) and generalization with explicit regularization removed (V5). These test components of the claims, although corrupted-label training fit is not reported.
record.authors_conclusion: The record correctly summarizes the corruption experiment but omits the broader conclusion: SGD's implicit regularization persists across NLP tasks, cannot be fully replaced by dropout, and remains evident with limited data or moderate label corruption. Stronger implicit regularization tends to favor smaller initialization ranges. The paper does not establish its own random-label training-fit result.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies SGD batch size and partially corrupts binary NLP labels to study implicit regularization; it does not reproduce the original image random-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported implicit-regularization gap weakens with increasing label corruption and is described as weakened at corruption level 0.3; results vary with batch size.

fits_no_version.finding: The generalization advantage of small batches persists at corruption probabilities 0.1 and 0.2, weakens at 0.3, and largely disappears near 0.4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SGD's generalization advantage over larger batches depends on label-corruption level.

record.problems: The paper's own corrupted-label results do not report training error, so they cannot establish whether the models fit the corrupted training sets. The corruption results are shown in Figure 6, and the supplied text gives qualitative descriptions rather than exact values.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were extracted: the paper's statements about fitting random labels refer to Zhang et al. (2016), and its own Figure 6 results concern generalization gaps across batch sizes rather than the training-fit and test-error outcomes specified in V4.

untested.parts: No own result establishes near-zero training error on completely random labels with unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
No measured comparison of convergence time across corruption levels or random versus true labels.
No experiments with shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect training fit under corruption and test performance reaching chance are not established by the supplied results. For binary labels, independent wrong-label flips produce fully random labels at p=0.5, not p=1.
Whether explicit regularizers prevent fitting random labels is untested. Weight decay and augmentation are not separately compared.
No learning trajectories distinguish learning shared patterns from memorizing noise.

missing.what: True-label Subj results with and without explicit regularization: Table 1 reports 100% training accuracy throughout; at batch size 1, test accuracy is 93.35% without regularization and 93.20% with dropout. Extract the paired results across batch sizes.

record.verdict_notes: The zero-training-error statement in Section 5.2 describes Zhang et al.'s findings. Figure 6's omitted corruption results are declared in rows_left_out, so they are not additionally listed as missing. No limits_scope verdict follows merely from untested components.

versions.untested_parts: The paper cites prior work on fitting random labels but does not report its own random-label fitting result.
The paper says convergence becomes slower as noise rises, but does not compare training time for random versus true labels or report the claimed constant factor.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiment.
The paper studies partial corruption levels and reports generalization trends, but does not report its own training error on corrupted labels or test error through the all-random endpoint.
Dropout is compared on true-label tasks, but the paper does not test whether dropout, weight decay, or augmentation prevent random-label fitting.
No experiment measures which labels or patterns are learned first over training.

relationships.condition: SST2 sentence CNN under partial binary-label corruption, especially larger batch sizes
relationships.reason: Section 5.2 reports progressively declining generalization as corruption increases, supporting the test-performance component. Based on text; Figure 6 results were explicitly left out of the record.
relationships.display_finding: Generalization declined progressively as corruption increased, particularly with larger batch sizes.

relationships.reason: Table 1 reports 100% training accuracy and 93.35% test accuracy without explicit regularization, versus 93.20% test accuracy with dropout. Based on text; corresponding rows are missing.
relationships.display_finding: Training accuracy reached 100% and test accuracy reached 93.35% without explicit regularization, versus 93.20% test accuracy with dropout.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
